sections.title: Core Theoretical Background
rows: One of the great 1819 odes. Famous for the concluding philosophical paradox: 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty,—that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.' Explores the theme of eternal art versus transience of human passion.

Explores themes of mortality, transcendence, and escapism through imagination and poetry. The speaker drinks the 'draught of vintage' and merges with the immortal bird's song, ultimately confronting the stark reality of 'Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget'.

Keats's final ode (September 1819). Celebrates the season of mellow fruitfulness without the melancholic despair found in his earlier odes. Personifies Autumn as a harvester, gleaner, and cider-presser living in harmony with nature's cycle.
On First Looking into Chapman's Homer

An early Petrarchan sonnet (1816) reflecting Keats's profound aesthetic epiphany upon reading George Chapman's translation of Homer. Famous for the geographical error regarding Cortez instead of Balboa staring at the Pacific Ocean.
When I Have Fears That I May Cease to Be

A Shakespearean sonnet expressing existential anxiety over dying young before achieving literary immortality and fully experiencing romantic love. Resolves temporarily by standing 'alone on the shore / Of the wide world, and do think / Till Love and Fame to nothingness do sink'.

items.definition: Coined by Keats in an 1817 letter. Refers to a literary creator's capacity to exist in uncertainties, mysteries, and doubts without any irritable reaching after fact and reason.
Keats's poetry heavily appeals to all five senses (tactile, visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory). Lines are dense with physical sensations, such as 'beaded bubbles winking at the brim'.
Deep fascination with ancient Greek art, mythology, and philosophy, heavily influencing 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' and 'Hyperion'.

A central philosophical duality in Keats where pleasure and pain are inseparable, best exemplified in 'Ode on Melancholy' where 'in the very temple of Delight / Veiling Her sole Hand has his sovran shrine'.

Examiners frequently trap students by asking who discovered the Pacific Ocean in 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer'. Keats historically erred by naming 'Cortez' instead of 'Balboa', but the exam question tests the exact name used in the text.

Students often confuse the exact composition dates of the great odes. Psyche, Nightingale, and Grecian Urn were written in spring 1819, Melancholy and Indolence slightly later, and To Autumn in September 1819.

Keats experimented with both Petrarchan (Italian) and Shakespearean (English) rhyme schemes in his sonnets. 'Chapman's Homer' uses the Petrarchan scheme (ABBAABBA CDCDCD), while 'When I Have Fears' uses the standard Shakespearean quatrain-couplet structure (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG).
Master the core themes of **transience**, **mortality**, and **eternity of art** across Nightingale, Grecian Urn, and Autumn.
Always remember Keats's signature critical concepts: **Negative Capability** and **Sensuousness**.
Memorize exact famous lines like 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty' and 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever' (from *Endymion*, though often linked to his overarching aesthetic).

upscNotes.content: For the UP Assistant Teacher Exam, memorize the exact lines ending Keats's odes, as matching quotes to poem titles is a very frequent question type.
Do not confuse Percy Bysshe Shelley's elegy for Keats ('Adonais') with Keats's own works. Examiners often mix up second-generation Romantic poets' works.

keyTakeaways: John Keats is celebrated as the most sensuous and aesthetic of the second-generation English Romantic poets.
His concept of 'Negative Capability' remains a cornerstone of modern literary criticism and aesthetic theory.
The 1819 Great Odes explore the tension between ideal permanent art and the painful decay of human life.
